units.text: These two machines get the same square tile. Each machine turns it once and flips it once. Surely that should leave the same result.
The left machine turns first. Watch the blue corner.
Then it flips across this horizontal hinge. The blue corner finishes at the lower left.
The right machine does the same two things in the opposite order. Before it moves, where do you think the blue corner will finish?
Flip first. Watch the blue corner move to the bottom. Now turn the tile a quarter-turn, and follow that same corner to its destination.
Different corners. The order changed the answer. Ordinary multiplication lets us swap three times five into five times three. These actions do not work that way.

But there is something remarkably tidy hiding here. Give either machine a hundred turns and flips, and the tile can finish in only eight different arrangements. We will prove why there are exactly eight.

We will build the arithmetic of these moves. It will tell us how to shorten a sequence, how to undo it, and which details we can forget without breaking the calculation. That last question will take us all the way to quotient groups.

Our two machines produced different arrangements, but both tiles still fit their square frame. Let's collect every move with that property. We are tracking the colored corners, so turning a tile counts as a new move even though its outline looks unchanged.

First, leave it alone. This sounds like cheating, but a machine needs a way to say: do nothing. Put that arrangement in the first slot. Now turn a quarter-turn, a half-turn, and three quarter-turns. Those fill three more slots. A whole turn takes us back to the first slot, so it does not give us a fifth rotation.

Next, flip the original tile across its horizontal hinge. Its colored corners occupy a different arrangement from every rotation in our first row. Put it at the start of a second row. Turn this flipped tile through the same four rotation choices. We now have eight arrangements.
Could there be a ninth? Perhaps a clever sequence of turns and flips that we have not tried? Rather than trying longer and longer sequences, watch just the blue corner and its orange neighbor.

The blue corner must land at one of the frame's four corners. Once we choose its destination, where can its orange neighbor go? The two corners share an edge. A symmetry preserves that edge, so orange must land at one of the two neighboring corners, not diagonally across the square.

That gives four choices for blue, and then two choices for orange. Once those are fixed, the other two corners are forced: each has a particular adjacency to the first pair. There are at most eight arrangements. Our rack already contains eight different ones. That proves the list is complete.

Now we can stop describing a move by the entire history of how we made it. Two sequences represent the same symmetry when they send every corner to the same destination. The machine might take a long route, but its final action is one of these eight.

Let's give the quarter-turn a short name: r. Let s mean the horizontal flip. We write a sequence as a product, with the rightmost action performed first. That is the same convention used when one function is placed inside another. So r s means flip first, then turn. We will keep the pictures beside the symbols until that order feels natural.

Try a calculation. Do a quarter-turn, and then another quarter-turn. The result is the half-turn in our rack. We write r squared. Three quarter-turns give r cubed. Four return every corner to its starting position. That result is called the identity, written e.

What does s squared do? Flip once, then flip again across the same horizontal hinge. Every corner returns. So s squared is also e. This does not mean s and r are the same move. It means these two particular sequences finish in the same arrangement.

Here is the calculation from our opening, expressed in this language. Turning and then flipping gives s r. Flipping and then turning gives r s. We can see different colored corners, so these are different elements of the rack. A product of actions remembers its order.

There is still a useful rule relating them. Flip, turn a quarter-turn, and flip again. The flips reverse our sense of clockwise and counterclockwise. The final result is the same as a quarter-turn in the opposite direction. Track all four corners to check it: s r s equals r inverse, which is also r cubed.

That rule lets us simplify complicated words. Whenever a flip sits to the left of a turn, we can move the flip past the turn if we reverse the turn. Pairs of flips cancel, and groups of four quarter-turns cancel. Eventually every word becomes a rotation, possibly followed on the right by one flip. Those are exactly the two rows of our rack.

We have found an arithmetic whose answers are actions. Combining any two entries stays inside the rack, and each entry has an undo move. A quarter-turn is undone by three quarter-turns. A half-turn undoes itself. Every reflection undoes itself too, though different reflections use different axes.

Before we call this a group, one distinction matters. Swapping two moves can change the result. Merely changing where we put parentheses cannot. If three actions are performed in the same order, grouping the first two into one instruction does not change what happens to any corner. That is associativity. It is a statement about grouping, not a license to reorder.

To see why this holds beyond a square, take any object and three functions. Applying the innermost function, then the next, then the last gives the same output whether we package the first two applications together or the last two together. Function composition is associative because the actual sequence of applications has not changed.

Closure, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element. Together these properties define a group. Our square symmetries give one concrete example. Numbers under addition give another: zero does nothing, and adding the negative undoes an addition. But positive integers under addition do not form a group, because most additions cannot be undone inside that collection.

These requirements are not a ceremonial checklist. Closure makes calculations stay within our vocabulary. Associativity lets us package a long calculation into steps. The identity gives a neutral action. Inverses let us solve equations by undoing operations. Next we will see how these four properties make deductions possible without knowing what the objects are made of.
It is eleven o'clock. Five hours pass. Where will the marker land?
Let's find out by moving five hours around the clock.
We land on four. Twelve steps bring us back to the start. On an ordinary number line eleven plus five is sixteen. On this clock, sixteen and four describe the same position.

Those numbers have not become equal as integers. They are equivalent for this particular purpose: each differs from four by a whole number of twelve-hour trips. If we were counting hours actually worked, four and sixteen would not be interchangeable. What counts as the same depends on the question.

The square gave us the group requirements. Now test them in a different machine: clock arithmetic. Start with a collection of moves and a rule for combining two of them. For the twelve-hour clock, the moves are advances by zero through eleven hours, and combining them means adding modulo twelve.
First, closure: combining two permitted moves must give another permitted move. Three hours followed by four hours is the seven-hour move. If the total passes twelve, wrap it around the clock.

Second, associativity: when we combine three moves, it does not matter whether we group the first two together or the last two together. Three plus four, then plus five, reaches the same clock position as three plus the result of four plus five. In either case the total is twelve hours, which is the zero move. This is one example, not a proof for every choice. In general, integer addition is associative, and taking a remainder before or after adding gives the same clock position.

Third, there is an identity move. Adding zero changes nothing. Fourth, every move has an inverse that undoes it. Advancing three hours and then nine more returns the clock to the start, so nine is the inverse of three.

Closure, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element: these are the group requirements. Notice what is not on the list. A group need not be commutative. The marked square showed that a turn followed by a flip can differ from a flip followed by a turn.

Do not confuse associativity with commutativity. Associativity changes the parentheses while keeping the moves in the same order. Commutativity exchanges the order of two moves. Symmetries can satisfy the first without satisfying the second.

Now the rules can solve a problem without knowing what the objects are. In a times x equals b, undo a by multiplying both sides on the left by a inverse. Associativity groups the inverse with a, leaving x equals a inverse times b. Multiplying on the right would generally give a different expression. The side matters.

Suppose a times x and a times y give the same result. Undo the common first factor on the left of both expressions. The identity disappears, leaving x equals y. This is cancellation. It also proves our equation has only one solution: two proposed solutions must agree. Right cancellation works by multiplying on the right instead.

Could a group contain two different identity elements, e and f? Because e does nothing on the left, e f equals f. Because f does nothing on the right, that same product equals e. One product cannot have two different values, so e and f are equal. The identity is unique.

Could a move a have two different inverses? Let b undo it on the left, and c undo it on the right. Follow this chain: b equals b times the identity, then b times a c, then b a times c, and finally c. We used only the identity rules and associativity. The left and right undoing moves must coincide, so the inverse is unique.

To undo a sequence, reverse its order and undo each move. If the product is a b, its inverse is b inverse a inverse. In the combined expression, b meets b inverse in the middle, then a meets a inverse. The cancellations work because we reversed the order, not because we were allowed to commute the moves. These deductions apply to every group. Now we can ask when a smaller collection of moves forms a group of its own.

What happens if we keep only the four rotations of the square? Combining two rotations gives another rotation, the do-nothing move stays, and every rotation can be undone by another one. This smaller collection is a group using the same operation. It is a subgroup of the square's symmetry group.
Now try a different selection: keep the identity, a quarter-turn, and a half-turn, but leave out the three-quarter-turn. Is this selection closed under the same operation?
No. A quarter-turn followed by a half-turn is a three-quarter-turn, and that move is missing. One failed pair is enough to show that this selection is not a subgroup.

A missing product is not a dead end. It tells us exactly what to add. Put the three-quarter-turn back, and the rotations close up again. Let's make that repair into a machine. Start with a few moves. Combine every pair, in both orders, and add any result that is new. Repeat until a full pass adds nothing.

Feed the machine the horizontal flip alone. Flip, then flip again, and every corner returns. So the only new move is the do-nothing move. The machine stops with two moves, and those two already form a group.

Now feed it the flip and the half-turn. One pass produces two new moves, the do-nothing move again and the flip across the vertical midline. A second pass finds nothing new. We have grown a four-move subgroup. Remember it. It comes back in the next chapter for a completely different reason.
Feed it the quarter-turn and the flip. The first pass adds four moves, the second adds the last two, and the machine holds the entire rack. Those two moves generate the whole group.

Try every possible starting collection, and only ten different groups ever come out. The do-nothing move alone. Five groups of two. Three groups of four. And all eight moves. Look at those sizes. One, two, four and eight. Never three, five, six or seven. Hold on to that pattern. Cosets will explain it.

Our machine checks every pair by hand. For a group with millions of elements we want something quicker. Here is a single test for any nonempty collection H inside a group. Take any two members a and b. Undo b, then do a. If that result, written a times b inverse, always lands back in H, then H is a subgroup.
Why is one test enough? H is not empty, so it has some member h. Feed the test h twice. Undo h, then do h again, and nothing has changed. So the identity is in H.
Next, feed it the identity and h. Undo h, then do nothing. The result is h inverse. So every member of H brings its undo move with it.
Finally, take any a and b in H. We now know that b inverse is in H as well, so feed the test a and b inverse. Undoing b inverse is the same as doing b. The result is a times b, so H is closed.

That gives closure, the identity and inverses. Associativity comes for free, because we are still using the operation of the big group. And every subgroup passes the test, so the test is exactly right. Now let's meet our four-move subgroup again, through a question about order.

Pick the horizontal flip s. Which of the eight square symmetries can we exchange with that flip without changing the result? Compare the two orders, and follow the numbered corners. What do you predict?

Start with the quarter-turn. The left tile turns, then flips. The right tile flips, then turns. This is the experiment we opened with, and the blue corner finishes in different places. The quarter-turn does not commute with the flip.
Now the half-turn. Turn halfway and then flip, or flip and then turn halfway. Every numbered corner finishes in the same place both ways. The half-turn commutes with the flip.
Let the scoreboard handle the rest. A move earns a check when the two orders agree at every corner, and a cross when even one corner disagrees.
Four checks. The identity, the half-turn, the horizontal flip itself, and the vertical flip. Four crosses. The two quarter-turns and the two diagonal flips. Is there a reason behind this list?

Draw the flip's mirror line, the horizontal midline. Now carry that line along with each move. The half-turn spins it end over end, and it lands on itself. A quarter-turn stands it upright. A diagonal flip stands it upright too. The moves with checks are exactly the moves that put the mirror line back where it was.

Here is why. Undo a move, flip, and then redo the move. Every point on the carried line ends where it started, so the result is the flip across the carried line. If the line came back to the original mirror, that result is just s, which says the two orders agree. If the line moved, it is a different flip, and the orders disagree.

The moves that commute with s form the centralizer of s. In our notation it is e, r squared, s, and r squared s. And look. It is the same four-move subgroup the machine grew in the last chapter from the flip and the half-turn.

Is a centralizer always a subgroup, in any group at all? Use the one-step test. Suppose a and b both commute with s. Multiply both sides of b s equals s b by b inverse, on the left and on the right, and b inverse commutes with s too. Now slide s from the right end of a times b inverse to the left end. It passes b inverse, then it passes a. So a times b inverse commutes with s, and the test is passed.

Now ask for more. Which moves commute with every move? That set is called the center. A move in the center must put all four mirror lines back where they were. Only the identity and the half-turn do that, and both commute with every rotation as well. The center is what all the centralizers have in common.

A cyclic group begins with a single move. Repeat it, run it backwards, and include doing nothing. Every position you can reach in this way belongs to the subgroup generated by that move. On our twelve-hour clock, let's use the move add eight. Before we calculate, predict how many different positions this move can visit.

Start at zero. Add eight and land on eight. Add eight again: sixteen wraps around to four. Add eight once more and we return to zero. From there the same three positions repeat. The subgroup generated by eight is zero, eight, and four. It has three elements, so the order of the element eight is three. The whole clock group has twelve elements. These are different meanings of order.

Why did we return after three steps? Each move contributes eight, so after m steps we are at eight m modulo twelve. Returning to zero means twelve divides eight m. The smallest positive m that works is three. The least positive return time is the element's order, and the distinct positions before that return are exactly the generated subgroup.

Now let's understand the general rule, not just memorize it. Let d be the greatest common divisor of n and k. Write n as d times n prime, and k as d times k prime. Those two primed numbers have no common divisor greater than one.

Returning to zero on the n clock requires n to divide m k. Cancel d, and n prime must divide m times k prime. Because n prime and k prime are relatively prime, n prime must divide m. The first positive choice is n prime itself. Therefore the order of k is n divided by the greatest common divisor of n and k.

This gives us a useful prediction. On a twelve-position clock, which moves visit every position? The formula says precisely those whose greatest common divisor with twelve is one: one, five, seven, and eleven. A single generator can trace the entire group in different orders. Eight cannot, because it shares a factor of four with twelve. A shared factor traps the walk in one smaller pattern.

There is a deeper fact: every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. Let's prove it in a way we can see. Suppose a group is generated by g, and H is a subgroup. If H contains only the identity, the identity generates it. Otherwise look at the positive powers of g that lie in H, and choose the one with the smallest positive exponent; call that exponent d. If a power is given with a negative exponent, its inverse is a positive power in H, so such a choice exists.
Take any power g to the m in H. Divide its exponent by d: m equals q d plus a remainder r, with r between zero and d minus one. Because g to the d is in H, its integer powers are in H too.

Multiplying g to the m by g to the minus q d leaves g to the r in H. A positive remainder would contradict our choice of d as the smallest positive exponent in H. So the remainder is zero, and every element of H is a power of g to the d. One element generates the whole subgroup.

But a group with four elements is not automatically cyclic. Consider the numbers one, five, seven and eleven under multiplication modulo twelve. Each is relatively prime to twelve, so each has a multiplicative inverse; their products stay in the set. Five squared, seven squared, and eleven squared all equal one modulo twelve. Every nonidentity element has order two. No single one can generate all four elements, so this group is not the same structure as the four rotations of our square.

The visual lesson is that repeating a move produces an orbit, and the first return measures its order. The arithmetic of greatest common divisors predicts that return on a clock. The subgroup proof works much more generally: divide exponents, then use the smallest positive step to rule out a remainder. Next we will make the moves themselves into permutations of labelled objects.

A permutation is a rearrangement that sends each item to exactly one position, with no collisions and no missing destinations. Imagine four numbered cards. We can describe a rearrangement by tracking where each label goes. Let's follow card one to its new position, then the card it displaced, until the trail closes.

Suppose one goes to three, three goes to four, and four goes back to one. We write the cycle one, three, four. The label two stays where it is, and we can omit that one-element cycle. The list is a loop, not a row of destinations: starting at three gives the same cycle, three, four, one. Reversing the direction usually gives a different permutation.

Now compute a composition. As before, the rightmost operation acts first. Take the cycle one, two, three after the swap one, two. Follow one: the swap sends it to two, then the three-cycle sends two to three. Follow three: it stays put under the swap, then moves to one. Follow two: it goes to one, then back to two. The composition swaps one and three and fixes two. Reversing the order gives a different swap.

To undo a cycle, run its arrows backwards. The inverse of one, three, four is one, four, three. If two cycles affect separate labels, they commute: each changes only positions the other leaves alone. Every trail in a finite permutation eventually returns to its starting label. It cannot first enter an earlier label in the middle, because that would give one destination two different inputs. So the trails form disjoint cycles. Their order and the starting point chosen within each loop do not change the permutation.

Those two separate loops answer a new question. Keep repeating the same permutation, the cycles one, three, five and two, six. On our clock, the first return was the order of the move. Here, return has a strict meaning, every card back in its own slot at the same moment. How many repetitions does that take? Predict before we run it.

Run it once, and the three cards step around their loop while the pair trades places. Run it twice, and the pair is home, but the three cards are not. At three runs the three cards are home, but the pair has split again. Runs four and five still leave a loop away. At six, both loops land home together, for the first time. So the order of this permutation is six.

Why six? The three cards are home only on multiples of three. The pair is home only on multiples of two. Every card home means a number on both lists, a common multiple, and the first such number is called the least common multiple. Card four never moves, so it adds no condition. Adding the lengths would give five, and at five neither loop is home.
Try a second one, the four-cycle one, two, three, four, with a separate swap, five, six. Multiplying the lengths says eight. Adding them says six. Work out the true return before the cards move.

The pair is home at two and again at four. The four-cycle first returns at four. So the whole row is home after four runs, the least common multiple of four and two. Eight is a return too, but it is not the first one, and six is not a return at all.

The loops have to be separate. In our earlier composition, the cycle one, two, three after the swap one, two gave the single swap one, three. Its lengths looked like three and two, but it returns after two runs, not six. Overlapping cycles interfere with each other. So first rewrite a permutation as disjoint cycles, then take the least common multiple of their lengths.

A transposition swaps just two labels. Every cycle can be built from transpositions. For example, the cycle one, three, four equals the swap one, four after the swap one, three, with the rightmost swap performed first. Check the path of each of the three labels. A cycle of length m can be built from m minus one transpositions, so every permutation can be built from swaps.
There may be many different swap descriptions of the same permutation. Can one description use an even number of swaps and another use an odd number? Predict before we prove it.

If the answer is no, parity belongs to the permutation itself, not to our chosen description. Here's one way to see why parity cannot change. Put distinct numbers x one through x n on the labels, and multiply all the differences x j minus x i for pairs with i less than j.

Swap the numbers on any two labels, and this product changes sign. The difference between the two swapped labels reverses. The two factors involving any other label exchange, sometimes both reversing signs, so their product stays the same. Factors that avoid both labels do not change at all. The magnitude stays the same.

After a sequence of swaps, that product has been multiplied by minus one once per swap. The final arrangement determines the final product, and the original product is not zero because the numbers are distinct. So two swap sequences reaching the same permutation must have the same parity. An even permutation requires an even number of swaps in every decomposition; an odd one requires an odd number in every decomposition. Swap counts add, so an even followed by an even stays even, and the even permutations form a subgroup.

Let's check that with cards. Swap one, two and swap three, four, which is even. Then swap one, three and swap two, four, also even. That makes four swaps, and the cards land as the double swap one, four and two, three. Two swaps can also reach that arrangement, and two and four agree in parity.

One more swap turns the count odd. Two odd moves make an even one, just as the swap one, two then the swap two, three builds a three-cycle. Write plus for even and minus for odd, and the signs simply multiply.

All the permutations of our labels form a group, since they compose and each one can be undone. Now use our subgroup test on the even ones. They are not an empty collection, because doing nothing takes zero swaps, and zero is even. Take two even permutations, a and b. To undo b, run its swaps backwards, which keeps the count. Then do a, and the counts add to an even number. So a times b inverse stays even, and the test passes. The odd permutations fail at once, because doing nothing is not odd.

How big is this subgroup on four labels? Four labels can be arranged in four times three times two times one ways, which is twenty-four. Follow every arrangement by one extra swap of the first two cards. Each even arrangement becomes odd, each odd one becomes even, and doing it twice changes nothing. So this pairing has no collisions and no missing destinations, and the two kinds are equally many, twelve even and twelve odd. The twelve even ones are doing nothing, three double swaps, and eight three-cycles.

Our square symmetries are permutations of its four corners, but not every permutation of four corners preserves a square. All twenty-four permutations form a group, and our eight square symmetries sit inside it as a subgroup. A quarter-turn is a four-cycle, so it is odd; a half-turn swaps two pairs of corners, so it is even. Now read the square's own moves as labels: r s is the swap two, four, and s r is the swap one, three. That is the same refusal to commute we saw on the tile.

Suppose a machine mixes a list by repeating one fixed rearrangement. Does the mixing go on forever, or does it eventually undo itself? Take the cleanest case, a perfect shuffle of ten cards. Cut the deck exactly in half, then interleave the halves so the top card stays on top. That is called an out-shuffle. It is one fixed permutation of the ten positions. How many out-shuffles bring every card home? Work it out before we run it.

Follow positions, just as we followed labels. Position one stays, and so does position ten. Two goes to three, three to five, five to nine, nine to eight, eight to six, and six back to two, which closes a six-cycle. Four goes to seven, and seven back to four, which is a swap. The lengths are six and two, so the least common multiple predicts six shuffles.

Now shuffle for real. After two shuffles the swapped pair is home, yet most of the deck is still out of place. After six, every card is home, exactly as predicted. One shuffle was enough to read the cycles, and the cycles gave us that number.

A full deck has fifty-two cards, and more arrangements than anyone could ever list. The out-shuffle sorts its positions into two fixed points, one swap, and six cycles of length eight. The least common multiple is eight, so eight out-shuffles restore the whole deck. Watch the staircase break apart and come back.

Now interleave the other way, so the top card drops to second place. That is an in-shuffle, and its fifty-two positions form one single cycle. The return takes fifty-two shuffles, six and a half times as long, from almost the same motion. Watching the hands would not tell you that, but the cycle lengths do.

So repeating one fixed rearrangement never mixes forever. It walks a closed loop, and the order tells us when the loop ends. The same shuffle also gives a wiring pattern for parallel computation. With eight wires, repeating it puts data back on their starting wires after three stages. Without switches to change the route, a fourth stage would only repeat the first.

A composition predicts the combined effect, and the inverse tells us how to undo it. Here, seven more out-shuffles undo the first. The group records what the moves do; it does not by itself guarantee that a physical device performs them without error. Suppose two neighboring cards trade places during one shuffle. That is one extra swap, so the eight shuffles now end on an odd permutation, and doing nothing is even, so the deck cannot be home. Next we'll ask when two groups with different-looking objects actually have the same structure.

The clock positions zero, one, two and three do not look much like rotations of a square. Yet the two systems can have exactly the same pattern of combinations. Think of a dictionary that translates every clock move into one square rotation and translates the results back without changing how combination works.

Send zero to the identity rotation, one to a quarter-turn, two to a half-turn, and three to a three-quarter-turn. Each clock position has exactly one partner, and every rotation appears exactly once. The dictionary is a bijection. Now try a calculation before we check the rule: what should two plus three on the four-clock become after translation?

Two plus three is one modulo four, so the dictionary predicts a quarter-turn. The translated moves are a half-turn and a three-quarter-turn. Together they make five quarter-turns, which has the same effect as one. In symbols, translating a sum gives the same result as combining the translations. This has to work for every pair, not just our example.

The general verification is short. Let the dictionary send k to r to the k. Then translating a plus b gives r to the power a plus b, and multiplying the translated moves gives r to the a times r to the b. Those are equal. Reducing an exponent modulo four changes nothing because r to the fourth power is the identity. The dictionary preserves the operation and is bijective. That is an isomorphism.

The operation and its labels must travel together. We are not claiming that a clock is physically a square. We are saying that questions phrased only in terms of the group operation have matching answers under this dictionary. Identity goes to identity, inverses go to inverses, and an element's order is preserved. Let's prove that last claim rather than just use it.

If g to the m is the identity, applying an operation-preserving bijection sends it to the image of g raised to the m, which must also be the identity. Conversely, if a power of the image is the identity, injectivity tells us the corresponding power of g was already the identity. The same positive exponents return each element, so their least positive return times agree. Infinite order is preserved too.

That gives us a quick way to rule out a false dictionary. The rotation group of the square has an element of order four: the quarter-turn. In U of twelve, every nonidentity element has order two. Both groups have four elements, but an isomorphism cannot send the quarter-turn anywhere while preserving its order. Equal size alone is not enough to make groups isomorphic.

Every group also has a faithful representation as permutations, even if its elements were not introduced as rearrangements. For each group element g, make a move on the group's own elements: send x to g x. This is a permutation because multiplying by g inverse undoes it. Performing the move for h and then the move for g sends x to g h x, so these permutations preserve multiplication.

Could two different group elements secretly give the same permutation? No. Watch what each move does to the identity: left multiplication by g sends the identity to g. If two moves were identical, their outputs there would agree, so the original elements would agree. We have built an injective operation-preserving map from the group into a permutation group. This is Cayley's theorem.

An automorphism is an isomorphism from a group back to itself: a relabelling that preserves every combination. For a four-clock, sending a position to its negative is an example; it exchanges one and three while fixing zero and two. These translations let us recognize shared structure across different representations. Next we will use equivalence classes to organize an entire group into equally sized pieces.
Imagine sorting integers by where they land on the twelve-hour clock. We will put numbers landing at four into one lane, and numbers landing at five into another.

Four, sixteen, twenty-eight and minus eight all land at four: their differences from four are whole multiples of twelve. Five and seventeen land at five. Different integers can occupy the same lane without becoming equal.

Call two integers equivalent when their difference is a multiple of twelve. Every integer is equivalent to itself: its difference from itself is zero. If one integer matches another, reversing the difference changes only its sign, so the match works in reverse.

And if the first integer matches the second, and the second matches the third, add their two differences. The first and third differ by a multiple of twelve as well. These three properties are called reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Now change the rule. Call two integers close when they are at most one apart. Zero is close to one, and one is close to two.
Does this rule have the transitive property? If the first is close to the second, and the second is close to the third, must the first be close to the third?

No. Zero and two are two apart, so they are not close under this rule. Being close is reflexive and symmetric, but it is not transitive. Chains of pairwise similarity do not automatically make equivalence classes.

Why does transitivity matter so much? Gather everything equivalent to one element, and call that collection its class. On the clock, the class of four holds four, sixteen, twenty-eight, minus eight, and every other integer that lands at four.

Suppose two classes share even one member, c. Then a matches c, and c matches b. Symmetry lets us read each link in either direction, and transitivity joins them into a link from a to b. Then everything linked to a is linked to b as well, so the two classes are identical. Two classes either coincide completely or do not touch at all.

Closeness breaks exactly this. The integers close to one are zero, one and two. The integers close to zero are minus one, zero and one. These groups share two members, yet they are different groups. Without transitivity, groups can overlap without coinciding.

So the classes of an equivalence relation cut the whole collection into separate pieces, and every element lies in exactly one piece. Twelve clock lanes hold every integer, and no integer sits in two lanes. It works backwards too. Any way of cutting a collection into pieces gives an equivalence relation, lying in the same piece.

Classes also let us build new objects. A fraction is written with a pair of integers, but one half and two quarters are different pairs naming the same number. Call a over b equivalent to c over d when a times d equals b times c. Plot each pair as a point, and every class lies on one straight line through the origin. The steepness of that line is the number itself. A rational number is one whole class.

Groups will do the same thing. A subgroup will define an equivalence relation. Its classes will be called cosets. And for the right kind of subgroup, those classes will become the elements of a new group.

On a twelve-position clock, start at zero and repeatedly add four. You visit zero, four, and eight before returning. These three positions form a subgroup H. Now move the whole pattern forward by one: the new set is one, five, and nine. Move it forward by two, or by three, to make two more patterns. These shifted copies are called cosets.
Before we list anything else, predict what happens if we shift H by four. Do we get a new set, or one we already have?
The shift sends zero to four, four to eight, and eight back to zero. It rearranges the same three points, so four plus H is H. Different labels can name the same coset.

The four distinct sets are H itself, one plus H, two plus H, and three plus H. Together they cover every clock position, and no two overlap. There are twelve positions, grouped into four sets of three. This particular clock makes the picture easy to see. Why must this happen for an arbitrary subgroup of an arbitrary finite group?

Now a group where order matters. In the square group, let H hold just the identity and the flip s. Multiply each member of H on the left by a move g, and you get the set g H, a left coset. For each rotation, the coset holds that rotation, and that rotation done after the flip. In our rack, each left coset is a column.

Now multiply on the right instead. H times r holds r and s r. But s r is the other diagonal flip, r cubed s. So the right cosets pair the quarter-turn with a different flip. Both ways cut the eight moves into four pairs, but they are different cuts. When order matters, left and right cosets need not agree.

When do two representatives name the same coset? Back on the clock, one and nine name the same coset, because the step from one to nine is eight, a move inside H. One and seven do not. That step is six, and six is not in H. Two representatives name the same coset exactly when the step from one to the other lies in H.

In multiplication language, write k as g times some correction h. The correction is g inverse times k. If it lies in H, then k H is g times h H. Multiplying H by one of its own members only reshuffles H, so k H equals g H. Conversely, k lies in its own coset, so if the two cosets agree, the correction lies in H.

So call g related to k when the correction g inverse k lies in H. This is an equivalence relation. Every element is related to itself, because the identity is in H. The relation reverses, because H holds inverses. And two corrections chain into one, because H is closed. So the cosets are equivalence classes, and two cosets either coincide or never meet.

Every coset is also exactly the size of H. Multiplying by g carries H onto g H, the way the shift carried the triangle around the clock. Two members of H cannot land on the same spot, because g h one equals g h two forces h one to equal h two. So each coset is a perfect copy of H, whether the group is finite or infinite.

Now count. A finite group splits into some number k of cosets, each the size of H. So the size of the group is k times the size of H. This is Lagrange's theorem. The size of every subgroup divides the size of the group. The twelve-clock is four cosets of three. And it explains the pattern from the subgroup machine. Three, five, six and seven do not divide eight, so no subgroup of the square can have those sizes.

Apply the theorem to the subgroup generated by a single element g. Its size is the order of g, the least positive number of repetitions that returns to the identity. So the order of every element divides the size of a finite group. In particular, g raised to the size of the group is the identity. This gives a useful test, but it does not say every divisor must occur as a subgroup size.

Be careful about reversing the theorem. A divisor tells us an allowed size, not a promise that a subgroup of that size exists. The even permutations of four labels form a group of twelve elements, but have no subgroup of size six. Six divides twelve; divisibility alone is not enough. Proving that absence needs tools we have not built yet. For now, keep the direction of our argument clear: a subgroup gives equal-sized cosets, and those cosets force divisibility.

On the clock, there is another useful observation. The cosets can themselves be added because choosing another representative does not change the resulting coset. But that is not automatic for every subgroup in every group. We have proved a partition and equal sizes; we have not yet earned the right to multiply cosets as group elements. That missing condition is normality.

Before we return to that question, we can combine two groups in a different way. Put two clocks side by side, and let a move turn each clock independently. The resulting pairs form a direct product. We can calculate in each coordinate and watch how two separate cycles combine into one longer orbit.

Imagine two clocks side by side. The first has four positions, the second has three. A state is an ordered pair: one position on the first clock and one on the second. There are four choices for the first coordinate and three for the second, so the combined system has twelve states. The order of the coordinates matters because they belong to different clocks.

A move adds a number to each coordinate, wrapping around its own clock. For example, start at three comma two and add two comma two. The first coordinate becomes one modulo four; the second becomes one modulo three. The answer is one comma one. The addition is componentwise: we perform the first operation in the first group and the second operation in the second group.

Why is the collection of pairs a group? Combining two pairs gives another pair, so it is closed. Associativity holds coordinate by coordinate. The identity is the pair of identities, and the inverse of a pair is the pair of inverses. This construction works for any two groups, even if their operations are not the same kind or are not commutative. It is called their direct product.

Now predict the orbit of one comma one. Each move advances both clocks by one. The first returns after four moves, and the second returns after three. When will both return together? It must be a common multiple of four and three; the first positive one is twelve. So this single pair visits all twelve states before returning. The direct product here is cyclic.

The argument generalizes. A pair returns to its identity precisely when both coordinates have returned. If the two elements have finite orders m and n, the pair has order the least common multiple of m and n. For the two clock generators, the least common multiple of four and three is twelve. If either coordinate has infinite order, the pair also has infinite order.

Does a product of two cyclic groups always make a cyclic group? Try two two-position clocks. There are four states. Every nonidentity pair returns after two moves, because each coordinate does. No pair has order four, so this four-state group cannot be cyclic. In particular it cannot be isomorphic to the four-clock, where advancing one position has order four.

This example is the same structure as U of twelve, the four units we met earlier. Each nonidentity unit has order two. Match zero comma zero to one, one comma zero to five, zero comma one to seven, and one comma one to eleven. Multiplication of the units matches coordinatewise addition. Check five times seven: it is eleven modulo twelve, just as one comma zero plus zero comma one gives one comma one.

The clock product is connected to the Chinese remainder theorem. When two moduli are relatively prime, sending an integer to its pair of remainders gives a well-defined isomorphism from the clock with product modulus to the product of the two smaller clocks. For four and three, the integer seven becomes three comma one. Adding on the big clock gives the same pair as adding on the two small clocks.

Why does the remainder map cover all pairs in this example? Repeatedly add one comma one: the orbit has twelve distinct pairs, exactly as many as the entire product. Thus every pair appears once. In general, relative primality makes the least common multiple equal the product; that proves the same finite-clock argument. With common factors, the orbit is shorter and some pairs do not occur.

So far we built a new group out of pairs. Can we find independent parts inside a group we already have? On the twelve-clock, take the subgroup zero, three, six, nine, and the subgroup zero, four, eight. Add one entry from each, reducing modulo twelve. Watch the table fill. Every residue appears exactly once, so every move has a unique description using these two parts. The subgroups share only zero, and their moves commute because clock addition commutes. Those facts let addition of parts match addition in the original group.

For general groups, the corresponding test requires the two subgroups to commute with each other, share only the identity, and together generate every element. Their sizes alone do not prove this. We have found an internal direct product: independent structure already living inside the group.

Next we return to the cosets we made earlier. They partition a group, but can we use them as the elements of a new group? We will try multiplying two cosets in the square symmetries and discover exactly why some subgroups allow the operation and others do not.

The cosets of a subgroup divide the group into equally sized pieces. It is tempting to treat each piece as one new object and multiply pieces by multiplying representatives. But a piece has many representatives. Before this can define an operation, every choice must lead to the same result. Let's see a failure using the square symmetries we already know.

Let r be a quarter-turn and s a reflection. Our convention is that the rightmost move happens first, and s r equals r inverse s. Take the subgroup H consisting of the identity and s. The identity and s name the same left coset H. Now multiply each of them by r. Do the two answers land in the same left coset?

The identity times r is r, which lies in r H. But s times r equals r inverse s. The left coset r H has two elements: r and r s. The element r inverse s is neither. So changing the representative of the first coset changed the proposed product. Multiplying arbitrary representatives does not define a coset operation here.

Here is the same failure with every choice at once. The coset r H has two members, so multiplying r H by r H gives four possible products. Color each product by the coset it lands in. If coset multiplication made sense, all four would share one color. Two products land in r squared H, and two land in H itself.

What went wrong geometrically? Conjugate the reflection s by a quarter-turn: turn back, reflect, then turn forward. The resulting mirror line is different from the original mirror line. The conjugated reflection lies outside the two-element subgroup. Our subgroup did not contain all its conjugates. That failure is exactly the obstruction we need to understand.

A subgroup N is normal in G when every conjugate g n g inverse of an element of N lies in N, for every g in G. Conjugating by g inverse gives the reverse inclusion, so conjugation actually carries N onto itself. Equivalently, g N equals N g for every g. This does not require each element of N to commute with every element of G; it requires the set to be preserved.

Now suppose N is normal. Define the product of two left cosets by multiplying representatives: a N times b N is a b N. We must prove that replacing a or b with another representative does not change the result. Suppose the alternatives are a n one and b n two, with both n values in N. Their product can be rearranged as a b times b inverse n one b times n two.

Normality puts b inverse n one b back in N, and closure puts its product with n two in N. Therefore the alternative product belongs to a b N. Since the left coset is unchanged by multiplying its representative on the right by an element of N, the proposed product does not depend on either choice. That is the whole point of the normality condition: it makes the operation well defined.

Normality is necessary as well as sufficient. If representative multiplication is well defined, H times a H must equal a H. Choose h as a representative of H; then h a belongs to a H, so a inverse h a lies in H. This holds for every h and a. Replacing a by a inverse provides the reverse conjugation too. Thus the subgroup must be normal.

For normal N, the cosets with this operation form the quotient group G modulo N. Associativity comes from G. N itself is the identity coset, and the inverse of g N is g inverse N. The quotient remembers which coset an element belongs to while treating elements inside the same coset as equivalent. The projection sending g to g N preserves multiplication.

Return to the square. Let R be the four rotations: identity, r, r squared, and r cubed. A rotation followed by another rotation stays a rotation; a reflection followed by a rotation is a reflection. Conjugating a rotation by a reflection reverses the angle, but it is still a rotation. Thus R is normal. Its two cosets are the four rotations and the four reflections.

Now look at the whole multiplication table of the square, all sixty-four products. Color each entry blue if it is a rotation and gold if it is a flip. Group the rows and the columns into rotations and flips, and the table falls into four solid blocks. The color of a product depends only on which blocks its two factors came from.
Shrink each solid block to a single cell, and a two-by-two table remains. That small table is the quotient group.

The quotient has just two elements. Rotation times rotation is a rotation; rotation times reflection and reflection times rotation are reflections; two reflections compose to a rotation. Its multiplication table is the same as the two-position clock. So the quotient is isomorphic to the group with two elements. It keeps the distinction between orientation-preserving and orientation-reversing moves, while forgetting which particular rotation or reflection was used.

Try the same thing with the subgroup made of the identity and s. Sort the rows and columns into its four left cosets, and color each product by its left coset. Now half of the blocks are mixed. The block for r H times r H is our four-product failure, sitting inside the table. There is no smaller table to shrink to.

That is a mathematical form of simplification. We choose distinctions we want to ignore, but only a normal subgroup lets us ignore them consistently while keeping a group operation. If we try the same shortcut with the subgroup containing just one reflection, the earlier calculation exposes the contradiction. The quotient is not a smaller picture of every detail: it is a precise record of the detail we chose to keep.

As a final test, ask what the projection sends every rotation to. They all land in the identity coset R. What does it send any reflection to? The other coset. The rotations are exactly the elements mapped to the identity; this set is called the kernel of the projection. Kernels are normal, which is why quotients and operation-preserving maps naturally fit together.

Abstract structure becomes useful when it captures the feature we need to test. As one example, consider the older ten-digit ISBN system. Modern ISBNs have thirteen digits and use a different check, but the older system gives us a particularly clean example. This is not a security system: it is an arithmetic check that catches particular copying errors. Its arithmetic happens modulo eleven, and its weighted sum is built from the additive group of residues modulo eleven.

Take the ten symbols of an ISBN, using values zero through nine, and allowing X for ten only in the final check position. Multiply the first value by ten, the second by nine, and continue down to weight one for the last. Add the results. The number is valid only when the total is divisible by eleven. A random ten-symbol string need not satisfy this rule.

Let's calculate one. The ISBN zero, three, zero, six, four, zero, six, one, five, two gives weighted contributions zero, twenty-seven, zero, forty-two, twenty-four, zero, twenty-four, three, ten, and two. The total is one hundred thirty-two, which is twelve times eleven. It passes the check. Passing does not prove that the ISBN was assigned to a real book.

Now make one copying error: change the fourth symbol from six to seven. That position has weight seven, so the total increases by seven, from one hundred thirty-two to one hundred thirty-nine. The new total is not divisible by eleven. The checksum catches this error without knowing what title the number was supposed to identify.

Why does that work for every single-symbol substitution? A changed symbol changes the weighted sum by its weight times the difference between the new and old values. Each weight from one to ten is nonzero modulo eleven. Distinct allowed symbol values differ by a nonzero amount modulo eleven. Because eleven is prime, the product of two nonzero residues is nonzero. So a single substitution cannot leave the checksum unchanged.

The primality matters here. In arithmetic modulo a composite number, two nonzero residues can multiply to zero: two times three is zero modulo six. We used more than the additive-group laws when we multiplied a weight by a difference. Modulo eleven also has the field property that nonzero factors do not produce zero. Keep that extra assumption visible.

What about swapping two different symbols? If positions i and j have weights w i and w j and values a and b, exchanging the values changes the total by the product of the weight difference and the value difference, up to sign. Distinct positions have distinct weights modulo eleven. Distinct symbol values have a nonzero difference modulo eleven. The product is nonzero, so this swap is detected.

That includes adjacent swaps, and in fact any two distinct positions, provided the swapped symbols form an allowed ISBN representation. Exchanging identical symbols changes nothing, so there is no changed number to detect. Here is a concrete failure. Change the first digit from zero to one, adding ten to the total. Also change the second from three to eight, adding forty-five. Together they add fifty-five, a multiple of eleven. The corrupted number still passes.

Multiple unrelated errors can cancel in the weighted sum. The rule detects every one-symbol substitution and every swap of two different allowed symbols, but it does not detect every possible corruption.

For a second application, look at a code that repairs an error instead of only noticing it. Hamming's code hides four data bits inside seven. Its sixteen allowed words form a subgroup of all one hundred twenty-eight seven-bit words. The operation flips bits position by position, a rule called exclusive or.

A received word with an error lies in some coset of that subgroup. One hundred twenty-eight words, sixteen in each coset. By Lagrange, there are exactly eight cosets. And there are exactly eight situations we hope to repair. No error, or one flipped bit in any of seven positions.

Each of those eight situations lands in a different coset. The checks are arranged so that the receiver can compute a three-bit label for the coset, called the syndrome. That label spells the position of the flipped bit in binary. In binary, the three places are worth four, two and one, from left to right. Here the label reads one, zero, one. So it holds a four, no two, and a one. Four plus zero plus one is five. Flip bit five back, and the word is repaired.

That label is a map onto the quotient group. It forgets which codeword was sent and keeps only the coset. So it has a limit. Flip two bits, and the word lands in the coset of some other single flip. Here two errors produce the label seven, the decoder confidently flips bit seven, and the result is a different codeword.

Related codes have long protected computer memory. Adding an overall parity check lets this code correct one flipped bit while reporting two instead of miscorrecting them. The quotient keeps exactly the information it was designed to keep, and nothing more.

Let's return to our square and clock. A group records how moves combine. A subgroup collects moves that remain closed under that combination. An isomorphism changes the description while preserving the structure. Cosets partition the moves, and a normal subgroup lets those pieces inherit an operation. Each definition solved a difficulty that appeared in a concrete example.

Try three exercises before the credits. Find the subgroup generated by six on the twelve-clock. Decide whether the four-clock and two two-position clocks can be isomorphic. Finally, explain why adding a subgroup's elements to a coset representative does not change that coset. Pause and work them out; the answers follow.

Adding six repeatedly reaches zero and six. The four-clock has an element of order four while the two-clock product does not, so they cannot be isomorphic. And multiplying a subgroup by one of its own elements permutes the subgroup: closure keeps the results inside, while the inverse recovers every element. These are small examples of a general method: follow the operation and ask what it preserves.
